title: War Against Midian
summary: God commands Moses to carry out vengeance on the Midianites for leading Israel into idolatry at Peor, as his last act before his death. Twelve thousand men go to war with Phinehas; they kill the five kings of Midian and Balaam, and bring back captives and plunder. Moses orders the execution of the adult women and boys, the soldiers are purified, the spoils are divided, and the officers bring an offering of gold because not one Israelite soldier was lost.
story: This chapter completes the story that began in chapter 25. There, while Israel was camped at Shittim, Moabite and Midianite women drew Israelite men into sexual immorality and the worship of Baal of Peor, and a plague killed twenty-four thousand. God then told Moses to treat the Midianites as enemies (25:16-18). Now, with the new generation counted and Joshua appointed, that command is carried out. The chapter also reveals something the earlier stories had not said: the scheme at Peor came through the counsel of Balaam (verse 16), the seer who in chapters 22 to 24 had been unable to curse Israel. He found another way to harm them. His death here closes his story. The next chapter turns to the division of the land east of the Jordan, some of it newly secured by this campaign.
historical:
The Midianites were a semi-nomadic people associated with the region east of the Gulf of Aqaba, in northwest Arabia, though their groups ranged widely across the Sinai and Transjordan. Genesis traces them to a son of Abraham by Keturah (Genesis 25:2). Moses' own father-in-law, Jethro, was a priest of Midian, and Moses had lived among the Midianites for forty years (Exodus 2 to 3). Not all Midianites were enemies; the group involved here seems to be those living in alliance with Moab near Israel's camp. The five kings of Midian named in verse 8 appear again in Joshua 13:21, where they are described as princes allied with Sihon, the Amorite king. Zur was the father of Cozbi, the Midianite woman killed by Phinehas at Peor (25:15).

This campaign did not end Midian. In the time of the judges, Midianites oppressed Israel for seven years until Gideon defeated them (Judges 6 to 8). The war described here was a limited action against a particular group near the plains of Moab.
cultural:
Holy war in Israel was treated as an act of worship under God's direction, and it carried rules of ritual purity. Phinehas the priest goes with the army, bringing the sacred vessels and the trumpets (verse 6; compare 10:9). Afterward, anyone who has killed or touched a corpse must stay outside the camp for seven days and be purified on the third and seventh days, following the law of chapter 19. Metal objects are purified by fire and water, other goods by water alone. Contact with death made a person unclean, even in a war God had commanded.

The division of the spoils follows a principle that later became Israelite custom: half to the soldiers who fought, half to the community that stayed behind (compare David's ruling in 1 Samuel 30:24-25). From each half a portion goes to God, one in five hundred from the soldiers' share given to the priest, and one in fifty from the people's share given to the Levites. The figures (675,000 sheep, 72,000 cattle, 61,000 donkeys, 32,000 girls) are very large, and they raise the same questions of interpretation as the census numbers in chapters 1 and 26.
literary: The chapter moves from battle to purification to accounting to worship. It opens with God's command (verses 1-2), describes the campaign briefly (verses 3-12), and then slows down. Moses' anger at the officers (verses 13-18) is followed by rules for purification (verses 19-24), a detailed division of the spoils with precise figures (verses 25-47), and finally the officers' voluntary offering of gold (verses 48-54). The careful bookkeeping of the second half is typical of Numbers, which likes lists and totals. The chapter's climax is the report that “not one of us is missing”, a sign of God's protection, and the gold is brought into the Tent of Meeting “as a memorial for the Israelites before the LORD.”

outline.t: God commands vengeance on Midian; twelve thousand go to war
Midian's kings and Balaam are killed; captives and plunder taken
Moses' anger and his order concerning the captives
The purification of soldiers, captives, and goods
The division of the spoils and the LORD's share

doctrines.note: The war is presented as God's vengeance for a deliberate attempt to lead Israel into idolatry, a scheme that cost thousands of lives. Scripture treats seduction into false worship as a grave sin against God and his people.

The root of the war is Peor, where Israel joined itself to Baal. The chapter shows how seriously the Old Testament takes the corruption of worship, and it names Balaam, a prophet who knew better, as its source.
Even in a war God commanded, those who killed or touched the dead had to be purified before returning to the camp. Death defiles, and the camp where God dwells must be kept clean.

words.note: Neqamah, vengeance. In the Old Testament vengeance belongs chiefly to God, as the just repayment of wrong. Here the war is “the LORD’s vengeance”, not private revenge. The same conviction lies behind the later words “Vengeance is Mine; I will repay” (Deuteronomy 32:35), which Paul quotes to forbid Christians from avenging themselves (Romans 12:19).

Mekhes, tribute or levy. The word, used only in this chapter in the Old Testament, names the share of the plunder set apart for the LORD. By taking a portion from both soldiers and people, the law reminded Israel that the victory and the goods were God's.

Zikkaron, memorial or reminder. The officers' gold is placed in the Tent of Meeting as a memorial before the LORD. A memorial in the Old Testament keeps something in remembrance before God and the people, here the preservation of every soldier's life.

christ: The chapter has no direct prediction of Christ, and its link to the larger story is one of contrast and fulfillment. The New Testament remembers Balaam as the model of a teacher who leads God's people astray: the letter to Pergamum warns against “the teaching of Balaam, who taught Balak to place a stumbling block before the Israelites so they would eat food sacrificed to idols and commit sexual immorality” (Revelation 2:14), and Peter and Jude use him as a warning against greed (2 Peter 2:15; Jude 11). The wars of Israel are also reinterpreted in the New Testament. Paul says the Christian's battle is not against flesh and blood but against spiritual powers (Ephesians 6:12). And the vengeance of God on sin, which falls in this chapter on Midian, falls in the gospel on Christ himself, who bore judgment for sinners, while Paul forbids believers to take vengeance, leaving it to God (Romans 12:19).

hard.q: How can a God of love command the killing of women and boys?
hard.a: This is one of the most disturbing chapters in the Old Testament, and honest readers should not look away from it. Moses orders the death of every boy and every woman who has had relations with a man, sparing only girls. Christians have responded in several ways. Some emphasize the particular setting: the Midianite women were the means of a deliberate plot to destroy Israel through idolatry, a plague had already killed thousands, and God as judge of all has the right to judge a people's sin, sometimes through human agents, as he later judged Israel itself through Assyria and Babylon. Others note the limits: this was a specific, divinely commanded act, not a pattern for later wars, and the Old Testament's laws of war elsewhere restrain violence (Deuteronomy 20:10-14, 19-20; 21:10-14). Still others see such texts as reflecting the language and customs of ancient warfare, recorded honestly by Scripture without being held up as models, and stress that Christ's teaching to love enemies governs how Christians read them. Many believers hold these responses together, confessing that God is just while admitting that the text remains painful. What should not be done is to use this chapter to justify violence today; the New Testament gives no warrant for that.

questions: Balaam could not curse Israel, but he found a way to lead them into sin. What does his story teach about the danger of spiritual compromise compared with open opposition?
Soldiers who fought in a war God commanded still had to be purified before rejoining the camp. What does that say about the effect of violence and death on the human soul?
How do you hold together passages like this one with Jesus' command to love your enemies?
